intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 (SMABF2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ASCC1 gene.

checks.explanation: The abstract reports homozygous/compound-het mutations across TRIP4 and ASCC1 together, without stating zygosity for ASCC1 specifically; the SMABF2 designation is not used.

paragraphs.text: Spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 (SMABF2) is a rare, severe autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder. It begins before birth and causes muscle weakness, multiple congenital contractures (arthrogryposis multiplex congenita), congenital bone fractures, neonatal hypotonia and respiratory insufficiency. Its outlook is poor and affected infants often die in the neonatal period (Knierim et al., 2016; Oliveira et al., 2017; Bohm et al., 2019; Giuffrida et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Oliveira et al. (2017) reported a female newborn with a severe neuromuscular disorder. She had generalized hypotonia, congenital bone fractures, no spontaneous movements and poor respiratory effort, and she died within the first days of life. Her karyotype and screening of several genes related to neuromuscular disease were normal. A male sib was later born with the same clinical presentation. Oliveira et al. (2017) concluded that the disorder lay within the spinal muscular atrophy or primary muscle disease spectrum.

paragraphs.text: Bohm et al. (2019) described the clinical, histologic and genetic findings in 3 families with ASCC1 mutations. All patients had severe prenatal-onset muscle weakness, neonatal hypotonia, arthrogryposis and congenital bone fractures. Muscle biopsies from the affected infants showed intense oxidative rims beneath the sarcolemma and scattered remnants of sarcomeres with enlarged Z-bands. The authors suggested that these changes may be a histopathologic hallmark of the disorder. Biopsies also showed variable fiber size and myofibrillar disorganization. EMG findings pointed to a severe congenital myopathy rather than motor neuron involvement.

paragraphs.text: In 4 families with prenatal-onset spinal muscular atrophy, arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, respiratory distress and congenital bone fractures, Knierim et al. (2016) used autozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing. They identified homozygous and compound heterozygous nonsense and frameshift mutations in the TRIP4 and ASCC1 genes. The mutations segregated with the disease and led to truncation or complete loss of the encoded proteins. Fibroblasts with ASCC1 mutations showed downregulation of genes associated with neurogenesis, neuronal migration and pathfinding (SERPINF1, DAB1, SEMA3D, SEMA3A) and with bone development (TNFRSF11B, RASSF2, STC1). Immunoprecipitation of the ASC-1 complex consistently copurified CSRP1, a transcriptional cofactor.

(2017) performed whole-exome sequencing and filtered variants under a recessive model. They identified a homozygous frameshift mutation (c.157dupG, p.Glu53GlyfsTer19) in the ASCC1 gene. paragraphs.text: In a stillbirth with SMABF2, Giuffrida et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the ASCC1 gene. Microarray analysis found a microdeletion of about 64 kb spanning 4 exons of ASCC1 (exons 7-10). Exome analysis then found a c.1027C-T transition on the other allele, which introduces a premature termination codon (arg343-to-ter; R343X). The authors stated that this was the first reported case of ASCC1 compound heterozygosity involving an exonic deletion and a nucleotide variant.
